faqs.question: What is the biggest danger for kids on Halloween night?
faqs.answer: Traffic. A JAMA Pediatrics study of 42 years of US crash records found pedestrian deaths 43% higher on Halloween evening than on the same evenings a week either side, and ten times higher for children aged 4 to 8.

faqs.question: What time is trick-or-treating most dangerous?
faqs.answer: Around 6 pm. The same study found pedestrian risk on Halloween peaked near that hour, so hold hands and cross only at corners for the first two hours out.

faqs.question: How many adults should go trick-or-treating with young kids?
faqs.answer: Our planning rule, not a published standard, is one adult per child under 5, one per two children aged 5 to 8, and one adult trailing a group of up to five aged 9 to 11. Plan for the youngest walker in the group.

faqs.question: Is reflective tape better than wearing light colors at night?
faqs.answer: Yes. A Cochrane review of 39 trials found fluorescent colors help drivers by day, while lamps, flashing lights and retroreflective material help at night. Put strips on wrists and ankles, because markings on moving joints also improved recognition.

faqs.question: Do I really need to check my child's Halloween candy?
faqs.answer: Yes, but for different reasons than the myth. No case of a stranger killing a child with poisoned trick-or-treat candy has been proven; the realistic risks are choking pieces for under-4s and allergens.

faqs.question: Can my 11-year-old go trick-or-treating without an adult?
faqs.answer: Many can, with a plan: a group of at least three, a fixed route, check-in texts at set times and a home-by time. Location sharing is a backup; a 2024 review found 33% to 69% of US families use tracking, but little evidence on what it changes.

faqs.question: Should my child wear a mask while trick-or-treating?
faqs.answer: Lift it off for every crossing at least. The JAMA Pediatrics letter lists masks that restrict side vision among the suspected reasons Halloween is riskier for walkers.

faqs.question: How do I keep my dog calm when trick-or-treaters come?
faqs.answer: Crate the dog or close it in a back room from about 5 pm and hand treats out on the step. We found no study of Halloween dog bites, so this is common-sense advice rather than measured data.

faqs.question: What should my house do to keep trick-or-treaters safe?
faqs.answer: Turn the porch light on, clear hoses and cables off the path, use battery tea lights inside pumpkins, and hand treats over at the step so children never cross a dark lawn.

faqs.question: Is it safe to post trick-or-treat photos online?
faqs.answer: Post after you are home, not live, and crop out house numbers and school logos. 48.3% of views of shared SubhSandesh pages happen on a phone, where a screenshot takes a second, so send the full set privately.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Trick or Treat Safety Tips, Ranked by the Size of the Risk

The trick or treat safety tips that matter most are about cars, not candy: hold young children's hands at every crossing, make them visible to drivers with retroreflective tape and a light, and plan a route with no mid-block crossings. US crash records show pedestrian deaths run 43% higher on Halloween evening, and ten times higher for children aged 4 to 8. Photos are the quieter risk of the night: 48.3% of shared SubhSandesh pages are opened on a phone, and 38.5% of our creators password-protect a page before sending it, a habit worth copying when pictures show your child's face and street. Below are eight tips ranked by the size of the hazard each one tackles, with the evidence behind every rank.

## What makes trick-or-treating risky?

Trick-or-treating is risky mainly because it puts small children on residential streets at dusk, in costume, during the busiest walking evening of the year. Traffic, not strangers or sweets, accounts for the deaths researchers can actually count.

The key study is a [2019 JAMA Pediatrics research letter by Staples, Yip and Redelmeier](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC6583441). It compared 5 pm to 11:59 pm on 31 October with the same hours one week before and one week after, across 42 years of US fatality records (1975 to 2016), and counted 608 pedestrian deaths on 42 Halloween evenings against 851 on 84 control evenings.

That works out to about 4 extra deaths per Halloween, with risk peaking around 6 pm. Keep the scale honest, though: absolute risk was small and fell from 4.9 to 2.5 deaths per 100 million Americans between the first and last decades studied.

Halloween lands on Saturday 31 October 2026 and Sunday 31 October 2027. A weekend date removes the after-school rush, so walk the route in daylight the day before.

## 8 trick or treat safety tips, ranked by the risk they address

Each tip lists the risk, what to do, the evidence and the ages it matters most for. Traffic comes first because only traffic has measured deaths behind it.

### 1. Hold hands at every crossing between 5 pm and 7 pm

- **Risk:** a child darting into the road from between parked cars or hedges.
- **Do:** hold hands at each curb, cross only at corners, and stop the group before every driveway.
- **Evidence:** in a [2024 Injury Epidemiology analysis of US crashes from 2016 to 2020](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC11010370), 43% of pedestrian injuries to children aged 0 to 9 were "dart-out" crashes. Halloween risk also peaks near 6 pm.
- **Ages:** 4 to 8 above all, the group with the tenfold rise.

### 2. Match the number of adults to the youngest walker

- **Risk:** one adult cannot hold three hands while also watching the road.
- **Do:** our planning rule, not a published standard: one adult per child under 5, one adult per two children aged 5 to 8, and one adult trailing a group of up to five aged 9 to 11.
- **Evidence:** in a [2026 virtual-reality study of 497 children aged 7 and 8](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13544160), training ran until each child crossed at adult competency. Parents' ratings of their child's crossing tracked real unsafe crossings; the children's own ratings did not.
- **Ages:** 4 to 11. Trust your read of your child over their confidence.

### 3. Put retroreflective tape where the child moves

- **Risk:** a driver noticing a dark costume too late to brake.
- **Do:** add strips to wrists, ankles and both sides of the treat bag, and give each child a flashlight or clip-on light. Lift masks off for every crossing; the JAMA letter lists masks restricting side vision among suspected causes.
- **Evidence:** a [Cochrane review of 39 trials by Kwan and Mapstone (2006)](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC8713592) found fluorescent colors help drivers by day, while lamps, flashing lights and retroreflective material help at night. Markings on moving joints, the "biomotion" layout, also improved recognition.
- **Ages:** everyone in a dark costume; on a hot or frosty night, layer under it so the tape stays on top. No trial measured crashes, so this buys earlier detection, not a proven injury cut.

### 4. Plan the route around crossings, not around candy

- **Risk:** mid-block crossings and streets without sidewalks.
- **Do:** finish one side of a street, cross once at a corner, then work back along the other. Where there is no sidewalk, walk single file facing oncoming traffic.
- **Evidence:** Staples and colleagues note that most childhood pedestrian deaths, on Halloween and all year, happen in residential neighborhoods, and name missing sidewalks and unsafe crossings as gaps.
- **Ages:** every group, tweens included.

### 5. Give tweens a phone plan, not only a phone

- **Risk:** a group of 10 to 13-year-olds without adults splitting up or running late.
- **Do:** a group of at least three, a fixed route, check-in texts at set times such as 6:30 and 7:30 pm, a home-by time, and location sharing agreed openly beforehand.
- **Evidence:** a [2024 review in Clinical Child and Family Psychology Review](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC11843666) found 33% to 69% of US families already use digital location tracking, but minimal data on its effects. The tracker backs up the plan; it does not replace it.
- **Ages:** roughly 10 to 13. Deciding when a child stops going at all is a separate question.

### 6. Sort the candy at home for choking hazards and allergens

- **Risk:** smaller than most parents fear. No case of a stranger killing a child with poisoned trick-or-treat candy has ever been proven.
- **Do:** before anyone eats, remove hard sweets, gum, nuts and tiny toys from an under-4's bag, bin anything unwrapped or homemade by people you don't know, and set allergens aside. A teal pumpkin marks a non-food bowl.
- **Evidence:** the measured harms of the night are on the road, which is why this ranks sixth.
- **Ages:** under 4 for choking; any age with a food allergy.

### 7. Shut the family dog away before the first knock

- **Risk:** a dog startled by masks, shrieks and a front door opening dozens of times.
- **Do:** households crate the dog or close it in a back room from about 5 pm and hand treats out on the step. Children never reach toward a dog in a doorway and step back if one appears.
- **Evidence:** we found no study of dog bites on Halloween night, so this rank rests on common sense, not data.
- **Ages:** small children, whose faces sit at a dog's height.

### 8. Light your path if you are the house handing out

- **Risk:** trips on steps, garden hoses, decoration cables and pumpkins in the dark.
- **Do:** porch light on, path cleared, battery tea lights inside pumpkins instead of open flame near costumes, and treats handed over at the step so nobody crosses a dark lawn.
- **Evidence:** no Halloween trip study exists. The lit porch also doubles as the usual sign that a house welcomes visitors.
- **Ages:** every visitor, especially children in long hems.

## How the eight tips compare by hazard, evidence and age

The table groups the eight tips by hazard, evidence strength and the ages each group matters most for.

| Tips | Hazard and its size | Evidence behind it | Ages most affected |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 and 2: hands, adult ratio | Traffic: deaths 43% higher, tenfold for ages 4 to 8 | 42 years of US fatality records | 4 to 11 |
| 3: tape and a light | Drivers detecting a child late | 39 trials, none measuring crashes | All ages |
| 4 and 5: route, tween phone plan | Mid-block crossings; groups splitting up | Crash data 2016 to 2020; tracking used by 33% to 69% of families | 10 to 13 for the phone plan |
| 6: candy sort | Choking and allergens; no proven stranger poisoning | Case history | Under 4, or allergic |
| 7 and 8: dogs, path lighting | Bites and trips | No Halloween study found | All ages |

The takeaway: the top three tips carry almost all of the measured risk, so if time is short, spend it on hands, adults and tape.

## Sharing the night without sharing your address

The last risk shows up after you get home: photos posted live can reveal a child's face, street and house number, and links travel. Pages average 11.1 views each, and 48.3% of those views happen on a phone, where a screenshot takes a second.

So post after you are home, crop out house numbers and school logos, and send the full set privately to the people who missed it. When a grandparent or a parent working late wants the night, the [interactive Halloween card with up to six photos](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) takes about 5 minutes, and its Kids tone stays spooky-cute with no gore and no jump scares.

For a fuller keepsake, the [cinematic Halloween page with a 60-second voice note](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) takes about 10 minutes, holds up to 12 photos, and for family and kids the No button never appears. Both offer an optional password at publish; for a birthday or another occasion, the [full template gallery](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) covers the rest.

## When these tips, or a card, are the wrong fit

Rural roads with no sidewalks and 50 mph traffic change the ranking: driving between a few known houses, or a community event, beats any amount of tape. The risk figures above are US data, so treat them as direction, not a forecast, for other countries.

Our pages cannot track a child, send an alert or replace a phone call, and they are English-only. On the night itself, a charged phone and an agreed check-in time do more for safety than anything we make.

## Sources

- Staples JA, Yip C, Redelmeier DA. Pedestrian fatalities associated with Halloween in the United States. *JAMA Pediatrics* 173(1):101–103; online 30 October 2018.
- Swedler DI et al. Injury and fatality risks for child pedestrians and cyclists on public roads. *Injury Epidemiology* 11:15; 11 April 2024.
- Morgan CH et al. An evaluation of parent and child perceptions about pediatric pedestrian safety skills. *Child & Youth Care Forum*; 12 August 2026.
- Kwan I, Mapstone J. Interventions for increasing pedestrian and cyclist visibility for the prevention of death and injuries. *Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews* CD003438; 18 October 2006 (abstract read).
- Davis IS et al. Digital location tracking of children and adolescents: a theoretical framework and review. *Clinical Child and Family Psychology Review* 27:943–965; 28 October 2024 (abstract read).
- SubhSandesh platform data, measured 24 September 2026.

sources.stat: Staples, Yip & Redelmeier, JAMA Pediatrics 173(1):101–103 (full text read on PMC): NHTSA FARS 1975–2016, 5:00–11:59 pm on 31 Oct vs same hours 24 Oct and 7 Nov; 608 pedestrian deaths on 42 Halloween evenings vs 851 on 84 control evenings; OR 1.43; about 4 extra deaths per Halloween; ages 4–8 OR 10.00; risk highest around 6 pm; absolute risk fell from 4.9 to 2.5 per 100 million between first and final decades; masks restricting peripheral vision listed among hypothesised risks; most childhood pedestrian deaths occur in residential neighbourhoods (lack of sidewalks, unsafe crossings).

Swedler, Ali, Hoffman, Leonardo, Romano & Miller, Injury Epidemiology 11:15 (CC BY, full text read): FARS + CRSS 2016–2020, 206,429 pedestrian injuries (36% in children 0–19); almost half (43%) of pedestrian injuries in children aged 0–9 were dart-out injuries.

Morgan, Stager, Smith, McClure, Davis et al., Child & Youth Care Forum (CC BY author manuscript, full text read): 497 children aged 7–8 in a VR pedestrian trial, training ran until adult competency; parent perception of real-world crossing significantly associated with baseline unsafe crossings and visits to competency; children's own perceptions showed less consistent, non-significant associations.

Kwan & Mapstone, Cochrane Database Syst Rev CD003438 (abstract only read): no trials on collisions/injuries; 39 trials on driver responses; fluorescent yellow/red/orange improves daytime detection and recognition; at night lamps, flashing lights and red/yellow retroreflective materials increase detection; biomotion-configured retroreflective markings enhance recognition; effect on safety unknown.

Davis, Thornburg, Patel & Pelham, Clin Child Fam Psychol Rev 27:943–965 (abstract only read): digital location tracking used by 33–69% of US families from childhood to emerging adulthood; much speculation but minimal data on ethical and developmental effects.
